title: Cauchy's theorem for finite groups and its classical corollaries
description: Cauchy's theorem (1845): if a prime p divides the order of a finite group G, then G has an element of order exactly p. Mathlib proves the existence statement (exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card, its Nat.card and additive variants) but records none of the classical packaged corollaries. This entry repackages the theorem and proves the consequences mathematicians actually cite: the subgroup-of-order-p form (the seed of the Sylow theorems), the even-order-implies-involution corollary (the p=2 case), the contrapositive coprimality certificate, and explicit 0-axiom witnesses in ZMod 6 realising Cauchy at the primes 2 and 3.

meta.author: Augustin-Louis Cauchy (1845); Lean formalization original

mathlibDependencies.description: Cauchy's theorem: for a finite group G and prime p with p ∣ Fintype.card G, there is x : G with orderOf x = p. The headline, restated as cauchy.
The Nat.card / [Finite G] form of Cauchy's theorem, restated as cauchy'.
The additive form of Cauchy's theorem (to_additive of the headline), restated as cauchy_add.
Nat.card (zpowers a) = orderOf a; turns a Cauchy element of order p into a subgroup of order p in cauchy_subgroup.
x ^ orderOf x = 1; combined with orderOf x = 2 gives the involution x * x = 1 in exists_involution_of_even_card.
orderOf (1 : G) = 1; used to derive x ≠ 1 from orderOf x = 2 in the involution corollary.
For prime p, p • x = 0 and x ≠ 0 imply addOrderOf x = p; certifies the explicit additive orders of 3 and 2 in ZMod 6.
Even n → 2 ∣ n; supplies the hypothesis of Cauchy at p = 2 in the involution corollary.

originalContributions: cauchy / cauchy' / cauchy_add: the existence form of Cauchy's theorem in the Fintype.card, Nat.card, and additive settings (Mathlib headlines restated as the baseline)

cauchy_subgroup: the structural form — p ∣ |G| yields a subgroup H ≤ G with Nat.card H = p, the cyclic group generated by a Cauchy element. This is the form that seeds the Sylow construction; Mathlib states only the element form.

exists_involution_of_even_card: every finite group of even order contains a non-trivial involution x ≠ 1 with x * x = 1 — the p = 2 case packaged as the classical involution statement underlying the theory of groups of even order. New content.
not_dvd_card_of_no_orderOf_eq: the contrapositive characterisation — no element of order p certifies p ∤ |G|, i.e. p is coprime to the group order. New content.

zmod6_involution / addOrderOf_three_zmod6 / addOrderOf_two_zmod6 / cauchy_zmod6_two / cauchy_zmod6_three: explicit 0-axiom witnesses in the additive group ZMod 6 (order 6 = 2·3) — the element 3 has order 2 (involution 3+3=0) and 2 has order 3, realising Cauchy at both primes dividing the order, verified by kernel decide (no native_decide).
meta.assumptions: None. Fully verified: 0 axioms, 0 sorries. The concrete ZMod 6 facts use kernel `decide` (not `native_decide`), so the file does not depend on Lean.ofReduceBool. Depends only on the foundational axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound via standard Mathlib lemmas.

overview.historicalContext: Augustin-Louis Cauchy proved in 1845 that a finite group whose order is divisible by a prime p contains an element of order p. It is the partial converse to Lagrange's theorem (a divisor of |G| need not be the order of a subgroup, but a prime divisor always is) and the base case of the Sylow theorems: from an element of order p one builds a subgroup of order p, then iterates to the full p-Sylow subgroup. The p = 2 instance — every group of even order has an involution — is the starting point of the structure theory of groups of even order, from Brauer–Fowler to the Feit–Thompson odd-order theorem.
overview.problemStatement:
Mathlib's `GroupTheory/Perm/Cycle/Type.lean` proves Cauchy's theorem in the form `exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card` (and its `Nat.card` and additive variants): a prime p dividing |G| yields an element of order p. But it stops at the element. None of the classical corollaries that working mathematicians cite — the subgroup of order p, the even-order involution, the contrapositive coprimality test — are recorded. Can these be packaged, and Cauchy witnessed explicitly in a concrete group?

**Answer:** Yes. From a Cauchy element x of order p, the cyclic subgroup ⟨x⟩ = zpowers x has order p (Nat.card_zpowers), giving the subgroup form. At p = 2 the order-2 element is exactly a non-trivial involution. The contrapositive is the direct negation of the existence statement. And in ZMod 6 the elements 3 and 2 realise orders 2 and 3 explicitly, witnessing Cauchy at both prime divisors of 6 with kernel `decide`.
overview.text: Cauchy's theorem (a prime dividing |G| produces an element of that order) is restated from Mathlib in its multiplicative, Nat.card, and additive forms, and then the classical corollaries Mathlib omits are proved: the subgroup of order p, the even-order involution, and the contrapositive coprimality certificate, capped by explicit 0-axiom witnesses in ZMod 6.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. cauchy, cauchy', cauchy_add: restate Mathlib's three existence statements as the baseline.
2. cauchy_subgroup: take a Cauchy element x with orderOf x = p; the cyclic subgroup zpowers x has Nat.card equal to orderOf x = p by Nat.card_zpowers.
3. exists_involution_of_even_card: from Even (Fintype.card G) get 2 ∣ |G| (Even.two_dvd); Cauchy at p = 2 gives x with orderOf x = 2; then x ≠ 1 because orderOf 1 = 1 ≠ 2, and x * x = x^2 = x^(orderOf x) = 1 by pow_orderOf_eq_one.
4. not_dvd_card_of_no_orderOf_eq: the literal contrapositive — if no element has order p then p cannot divide |G|, else Cauchy would produce one.
5. ZMod 6 witnesses: 3 + 3 = 0 and 3 ≠ 0 by decide give the involution; addOrderOf_eq_prime upgrades these (and the p = 3 analogue for the element 2) to addOrderOf 3 = 2, addOrderOf 2 = 3; cauchy_zmod6_two/three fire the general theorem on ZMod 6 since 2, 3 ∣ 6.
keyInsights: **Mathlib stops at the element; the corollaries are the content**: the three existence statements are direct re-exports, so the genuine contribution is the packaged subgroup / involution / contrapositive forms that Mathlib does not record.

**An element of order p IS a subgroup of order p**: the cyclic group it generates, zpowers x, has cardinality orderOf x, so Cauchy's element form upgrades for free to the subgroup form that the Sylow theory actually consumes.

**Even order ⟹ involution is just Cauchy at p = 2**: an element of order 2 is precisely a non-trivial self-inverse element, x * x = x^(orderOf x) = 1, making the classical involution lemma a one-line specialisation.

**`decide` sees the involution but not the order**: `addOrderOf` does not reduce under kernel computation, so the explicit orders in ZMod 6 are certified through addOrderOf_eq_prime (from the decidable facts p • x = 0 and x ≠ 0) rather than by deciding `addOrderOf x = p` directly — keeping the file free of `native_decide` and hence of Lean.ofReduceBool.

**The contrapositive is a certificate, not just a restatement**: since G is a `Fintype`, `¬∃x, orderOf x = p` in `not_dvd_card_of_no_orderOf_eq` is a decidable finite search over the (finitely many) element orders of G — so the lemma yields an actual coprimality test for p ∤ |G| that never has to compute `Nat.card G` at all, only enumerate orders.
prerequisites: Finite groups, Lagrange's theorem, and the order of an element (orderOf)
Cyclic subgroups generated by a single element (Subgroup.zpowers) and their cardinality
The additive group ZMod n and additive order (addOrderOf)
The Sylow theorems, for which Cauchy's theorem is the base case

mainTheorems.name: cauchy_subgroup
mainTheorems.description: Subgroup form of Cauchy: p ∣ |G| (p prime) yields a subgroup H ≤ G with Nat.card H = p — the cyclic group zpowers x of a Cauchy element, whose cardinality is orderOf x = p (Nat.card_zpowers). The form that seeds the Sylow construction; Mathlib states only the element form.
mainTheorems.leanType: [Group G] [Finite G] (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hdvd : p ∣ Nat.card G) : ∃ H : Subgroup G, Nat.card H = p

mainTheorems.name: exists_involution_of_even_card
mainTheorems.description: Even order implies an involution: every finite group of even order contains x ≠ 1 with x·x = 1. The p = 2 case of Cauchy (Even.two_dvd → cauchy 2 → orderOf x = 2 → x² = x^(orderOf x) = 1). New content underlying the theory of groups of even order.
mainTheorems.leanType: [Group G] [Fintype G] (h : Even (Fintype.card G)) : ∃ x : G, x ≠ 1 ∧ x * x = 1

mainTheorems.name: cauchy
mainTheorems.description: Cauchy's theorem (Fintype.card form): a prime p dividing |G| yields an element of order exactly p. Mathlib's exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card restated as the baseline (also cauchy' for Nat.card and cauchy_add for additive groups).
mainTheorems.leanType: [Group G] [Fintype G] (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (hdvd : p ∣ Fintype.card G) : ∃ x : G, orderOf x = p

mainTheorems.name: not_dvd_card_of_no_orderOf_eq
mainTheorems.description: Contrapositive coprimality certificate: if G has no element of order p then p ∤ |G|. Literal negation of Cauchy (assuming p ∣ |G| would produce the missing element). New content.
mainTheorems.leanType: [Group G] [Fintype G] (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (h : ¬ ∃ x : G, orderOf x = p) : ¬ p ∣ Fintype.card G

mainTheorems.name: addOrderOf_three_zmod6
mainTheorems.description: Explicit Cauchy witness at p = 2 in ZMod 6: the element 3 has additive order 2 (the involution 3+3=0), certified via addOrderOf_eq_prime from decidable facts — kernel decide, no native_decide.

mainTheorems.name: cauchy_zmod6_three
mainTheorems.description: The general theorem fired at p = 3 in ZMod 6: an element of additive order 3 exists (since 3 ∣ 6). Companion cauchy_zmod6_two does the same at p = 2.

conclusion.summary: Cauchy's theorem (a prime dividing |G| produces an element of that order) is restated from Mathlib in its multiplicative, Nat.card, and additive forms, then the classical corollaries Mathlib omits are proved: the subgroup of order p (the Sylow seed), the even-order involution (the p = 2 case), and the contrapositive coprimality certificate — capped by explicit 0-axiom witnesses in ZMod 6 realising Cauchy at both primes 2 and 3 via kernel decide.
implications: An element of order p and a subgroup of order p are interchangeable data: zpowers x has cardinality orderOf x, so cauchy_subgroup upgrades the element form for free to the structural form the Sylow theory actually consumes — making this entry the recorded base case of Sylow.

The even-order involution is a one-line specialization of Cauchy at p = 2, yet it is the engine of the structure theory of groups of even order (Brauer–Fowler, Feit–Thompson); recording it as a named lemma exposes that lineage.

Genuine 0-axiom concreteness needs care: addOrderOf does not reduce under the kernel, so the ZMod 6 orders are certified through addOrderOf_eq_prime from decidable p•x = 0 / x ≠ 0 facts rather than by deciding addOrderOf directly — keeping the file free of native_decide and Lean.ofReduceBool.
openQuestions: Package the iterated form: from cauchy_subgroup, build the full p-Sylow subgroup of order p^k (p^k ‖ |G|) as a named corollary, making the Cauchy→Sylow climb explicit rather than implicit.

Generalize the contrapositive certificate to a decidable test on concrete groups: an algorithm that, given a finite group presentation, certifies the set of primes dividing |G| by exhibiting order-p elements (or their absence).

crossReferences.description: Child entry continuing the Cauchy corollary program with further packaged consequences.
Cauchy's theorem (specifically its subgroup form cauchy_subgroup) is the base case of the Sylow theorems: from a subgroup of order p one climbs to the full p-Sylow subgroup.
Cauchy is the partial converse of Lagrange's theorem: Lagrange says subgroup orders divide |G|; Cauchy says every prime divisor of |G| is realized as a (cyclic) subgroup order.

All by kernel decide, no native_decide.
